This is Buffalo dance. Traditional / Historical.
on_screen: Title card: Buffalo dance · United States · Traditional / Historical

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Buffalo Dance traditionally coincided with the annual return of the buffalo herds among Plains Native groups including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee, and Omaha.
The bison was central to Plains Native society, making the dance vital for securing food, resources, and community survival.
In 1894, a 16-second silent film recorded people performing the dance, making it one of the earliest films featuring Native Americans.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The ceremony coincided with the return of buffalo herds, incorporating feasts and spiritual requests for abundance.
It also functioned as a section of larger ceremonies like the Sun Dance or as a curing dance calling on the spirit of the buffalo for healing.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants traditionally wore buffalo and other animal skins.
Among the Chaui Band of Pawnee, the dance took place inside a large earth lodge facing east, with a painted buffalo skull resting on a folded blanket in front of an altar opposite the entrance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Historical figures associated with Pawnee ceremonial performances include Wicita Blain (a blind singer of the Skidi Band who inherited Buffalo dance songs), Mrs. Effie Blain, John Luwak (chief of the Chaui Band), and Stacy Matlock (who managed the Painting the Buffalo Skull ceremony).
The dance was practiced with distinct societal rules across multiple Plains tribes, including the Mandan, Sioux, Cheyenne, Pawnee (Chaui and Skidi bands), and Omaha.
The songs and ceremonial rights of the Buffalo Dance were passed down through inheritance within specific tribal societies, such as the Buffalo Society of the Pawnee.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The Buffalo Dance is a sacred ritual with spiritual and curing functions; ceremonial details and song rights are restricted to authorized members of tribal societies.
